title: A scope that survives the first client meeting
metaTitle: A scope that survives the meeting
excerpt: Write the pages, the states, and what is out before the first client meeting. A new idea after that is either a swap or a later phase, not a silent addition.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby, the pages and states written down before a meeting can widen them.
caption: Wireframes and a blue pen. Write the pages, the states, and what is out. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a website scope include?
faqs.answer: Name the pages, the job of each page, and the states that are in, such as empty, error, success, and the phone view. Write an out list in the same document. A word like website, with no nouns under it, is not a scope.

faqs.question: What should happen when someone has a new idea mid-project?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a swap of similar weight, or park it as a later phase. Agree that rule while the first meeting is still friendly. Absorbing every idea into the current release is how the date slips and QA gets thin.

faqs.question: Are empty and error states part of the design?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the page can be empty or wrong. A picture of the happy path leaves the engineer to invent the rest, and that invention is scope whether you planned it or not. Mobile is a state of every page, not a second website.

markdown:
A scope that survives the first meeting is a list of pages, a list of states, and a list of what is out. When a new idea appears, it is either a swap for something on the list or a later phase. Website scope creep is what happens when those lists were never written, and every new sentence feels free.

Write the lists before you fall in love with a concept. Hope is not a line item. A pleasant workshop can still produce a document a founder and a studio can reread in week six without arguing about memory.

## Pages, not a vibe

Name the pages. Homepage. A services or product page. A proof page. A contact or booking path. A basic article template, if you are publishing. For a shop: index, product, cart, checkout, and the policy pages you are willing to honor. For a product: the marketing page, the sign-in, the first-run path, and the one workflow the release is about.

Each page needs a job in one sentence. If you cannot write the job, the page is a hunch. Hunches can go on a later list. They do not go on this one.

Count them. A first release for a small company is often a handful of templates, not forty unique layouts. Templates are your friend. A case study template that can hold six projects is one scope line. Six bespoke case studies with different layouts are six.

Say which pages are new, which are redesigned, and which are left alone. "The website" is not a scope. A founder hears a new company. A studio hears a homepage. Write the nouns.

Include the unglamorous pages on purpose. Search results, the 404, the account email, the invoice, the password reset. If they are in, they get designed. If they are out, say they will use a plain default. Silence means you will argue about them later, usually the week of launch.

## States, or the page is a poster

Every important page has states. Write them down.

A form has empty, typing, error, and success. A shop grid has results, no results, and loading. A product has available, sold out, and a variant. A dashboard has first visit, data, and no permission. A marketing page has the ordinary view and the view with a campaign banner, if you truly need both in this release.

The happy path is the picture everyone shares in the meeting. The other states are the work. A flat picture of the happy path forces the engineer to invent the rest. That invention is scope, whether you planned it or not.

Mobile is not a separate website. It is a state of every page. Say that type, navigation, and the primary action must work on a phone. If a specific page has a different mobile structure, name that page. "Responsive" as a single word has started more arguments than it has ended.

Accessibility belongs in the same list, at the level you mean. Text for images that carry meaning. Focus states. Contrast that you can read. Forms that can be completed without a mouse. The WCAG overview organizes the standard under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. You do not need to paste the standard into the statement of work. You do need to say that those principles are part of done, so they are not treated as a favor at the end.

## What is out

Write the out list in the same document, in the same plain language. It will feel blunt. It is kinder than a fight.

Common outs for a first site: a new brand from zero, illustration of every section, a native app, a customer community, localization into three languages, a custom checkout if a platform checkout would do, a blog with a year's backlog, and an integrations marketplace. Your outs will differ. The point is that they are written.

Also write the outs that are really "later." A second audience's landing page. A partner directory. A resources library with twenty guides. These are legitimate. They are not free additions because someone thought of them while looking at a wireframe.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a site has a primary purpose. The out list protects that purpose. A site that tries to launch every idea has no purpose a stranger can see. Cutting is how the purpose stays visible.

Say who can add to the out list. Usually the same person who can approve a swap. If anyone in a meeting can add a page by enthusiasm, you do not have a scope. You have a transcript.

## A new idea is a swap or a phase

New ideas will come. They should. The rule is the part that has to be agreed in the first meeting, while everyone still likes each other.

A swap removes something of similar weight and adds the new thing. A new page in, an old page out. A new state in, a decorative illustration out. Say what "similar weight" means in your project: a template, a section, a workflow. Do not pretend a checkout and a favicon are the same weight.

A phase parks the idea in writing, with a sentence, and leaves this release alone. The idea is not rejected forever. It is rejected for this date. That distinction lets a founder hear "not now" without hearing "you were wrong to want it."

What you should not do is absorb the idea into the current release and hope the date still holds. That is the creep. It shows up as late nights, a thinner QA pass, and a quiet argument about whether the new page was "always implied." Implied is the word that ruins scopes. If it was not on the list, it was not implied.

Hanabi's working practice is to design and build against that list, in Figma first when the structure is cheap to change, then in production code. Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind are the usual materials. They do not make scope optional. They make a clear scope shippable. Motion is specified where it matters, with a reduced-motion state, which is itself a state on the list rather than a surprise.

Write the rule into the proposal in two sentences. New work is a swap or a later phase. The date and the fee assume the lists above. A founder who will not accept those sentences is telling you the project is a different shape. Better to learn that before the kickoff.

## The meeting that tries to widen it

The first client meeting is where the lists get tested. Bring them. Read the out list aloud. It will feel awkward. It is also the conversation that keeps the date intact.

Ask each person what they think they are getting. You will hear pages nobody wrote down. Add them to a parking list in the room, visibly, so they are not lost and not silently included. At the end, confirm the in list again.

Watch for the phrase "while we're in there." It is how a footer tweak becomes a new information architecture. Answer it with the rule. Swap or phase. You can be warm and still use the rule. Warmth without the rule is how the scope dissolves.

If a stakeholder cannot attend, the decider in the room has to be allowed to decide. Otherwise every list is provisional, and provisional lists do not survive contact with the absent person. Say that at the start. If the decider is missing, reschedule. A meeting that cannot close is not a review. It is a preview of the stall.

Keep notes in a place both sides can open later. On a Hanabi project the client portal holds docs and updates after delivery, and the same habit should start during the work. The scope lives there, dated. When a swap happens, the doc changes. Memory is not a version history.

## A scope is also a definition of done

Attach the checks to the list. Each page has been reviewed on a phone. Forms submit and fail in a way a person can understand. The basic title and description exist. The client can edit the words that change. Access sits with the client. The out list is still out.

This is quieter than a creative presentation. It is the document you will be glad to have when a new stakeholder arrives with a mood board in week five. You can welcome the mood board onto the later list. You can point at the pages you already agreed to finish.

If the offer itself has changed, the scope is the wrong argument. A redesign that keeps the offer is one project. A new offer needs new sentences before anyone redraws the layout. The piece on [the difference between a redesign and a new offer](/blog/the-difference-between-a-redesign-and-a-new-offer) is the next read if the meeting is really a strategy meeting wearing a wireframe.

When you want to put pages, states, and outs on one table with a studio, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the pages you think you need and the ones you hope you can ignore. The call should leave you with a shorter list, and with the rule for what happens when a good idea arrives late.
